terms.gloss: send money to another place by exchange, without carrying it: transfer
evidence: Cic. Att. 12.24.1: Athēnīs permūtārīne possit an ipsī ferendum sit
terms.comment: Cicero’s word for getting his son’s allowance to Athens through Atticus’s agents, who paid it out there, instead of sending coin (Lewis & Short: “of payments by exchange”). Of a modern bank transfer its use is ours. In other contexts permūtāre is to swap (see “trade”).

phrases.latin: sed quaerō, quod illī opus erit, Athēnīs permūtārīne possit an ipsī ferendum sit
phrases.english: but I want to know whether what he will need can be transferred to Athens, or whether he must take it with him

phrases.latin: Pecūniam tibi per argentāriam permūtāvī; crās praestō erit.
phrases.english: I’ve transferred the money to you through the bank; it’ll be there tomorrow.

phrases.latin: Pecūniam in ratiōnem tuam argentāriam mīsī.
phrases.english: I’ve sent the money to your bank account.
